Four-day school weeks
passage:
In some countries, a number of schools, especially in rural areas, have switched from a five-day week to a four-day week. Students attend school for slightly longer hours from Monday to Thursday and have Friday off. School districts that have adopted this schedule say that it helps them save money on transportation, heating, and other running costs.

Supporters also argue that the shorter week can benefit teachers and students. Schools in rural areas often struggle to hire teachers, and offering a four-day week has helped some districts attract new staff. Students can use the extra day for part-time jobs, medical appointments, or family activities, which may reduce absences on school days.

However, some researchers have raised concerns. Studies suggest that, in some cases, students in four-day schools made slower progress in subjects such as math. Working parents may also find it difficult to arrange childcare on the day off, and children from low-income families may lose access to free school meals. Experts say that schools considering the change need to provide activities and support on the fifth day.

topic: Hydrogen-powered trucks
passage:
Trucks are responsible for a large share of greenhouse gas emissions from road transportation. While electric batteries work well for cars, they are heavy and take a long time to charge, which makes them less practical for large trucks that travel long distances. For this reason, some manufacturers are developing trucks that run on hydrogen fuel cells, which produce only water as a by-product.

Supporters point out that hydrogen trucks can be refueled in about fifteen minutes, similar to diesel trucks, and can travel more than 800 kilometers on a single tank. This allows logistics companies to keep their delivery schedules without long breaks for charging.

However, there are major obstacles. Hydrogen is currently expensive to produce, and most of it is made from natural gas, which releases carbon dioxide. There are also very few hydrogen fueling stations, and building a network across a country would require huge investment. Experts say that hydrogen trucks will only become widespread if governments provide financial support and if cleaner methods of producing hydrogen become cheaper.

topic: Hiring older workers
passage:
In many countries, the population is aging, and companies are facing shortages of workers. As a result, some businesses have started to actively hire people in their sixties and seventies. Some companies have also raised their retirement age or created programs that allow employees to continue working part-time after retirement.

Companies that employ older workers say that they bring valuable experience and skills. Older employees are often reliable and can train younger staff. For the workers themselves, continuing to work can provide income, a sense of purpose, and opportunities for social contact, which may help them stay healthy.

However, there are challenges. Some older workers may find physically demanding jobs difficult, and they may need more time to learn new technology. In addition, some younger workers worry that if older employees stay longer, there will be fewer opportunities for promotion. Experts suggest that companies should offer flexible working hours and training programs so that employees of all ages can work together effectively.

topic: Charging tourists entry fees
passage:
Some popular tourist destinations have started charging visitors a fee to enter. For example, a famous historic city in Europe now requires day-trippers to pay a small fee during busy periods, and some mountain areas charge hikers to use their trails. The money collected is often used to maintain facilities and protect the local environment.

Supporters say that entry fees can help reduce overcrowding. When too many tourists visit at the same time, streets become congested, and residents find it difficult to live their daily lives. Fees may encourage some visitors to come at quieter times or to visit other places instead.

However, critics argue that the fees are too small to have much effect on the number of visitors. They also say that charging people to enter a city could make it seem like a theme park rather than a place where people live. Some local businesses worry that fewer tourists will mean less income. Experts say that fees should be combined with other measures, such as limiting the number of tour groups and promoting less famous destinations.

topic: School uniforms
passage:
In many countries, students are required to wear school uniforms. However, in recent years, some schools have reconsidered this rule. A number of schools now allow students to choose between different types of uniforms, such as skirts or trousers, and some schools have abolished uniforms entirely.

Supporters of uniforms say that they help create a sense of belonging and reduce pressure on students to wear fashionable clothes. They also argue that uniforms can save families money, because parents do not need to buy many different outfits for school, and they make it easier for teachers to identify students during school trips.

On the other hand, critics say that uniforms can be expensive, especially when they must be bought from specific stores. Some students also feel uncomfortable wearing clothes that do not match their gender identity or that are unsuitable for hot weather. As a result, many schools have started to involve students and parents in discussions about uniform rules, and some have introduced more comfortable and flexible options.

topic: Digital textbooks
passage:
Many schools have begun using digital textbooks instead of traditional printed books. Students can read the textbooks on tablets or computers, and the digital versions often include videos, audio recordings, and interactive exercises. Some governments have encouraged this change as part of efforts to improve education through technology.

Supporters say that digital textbooks make learning more engaging and allow students to study at their own pace. They can be updated easily when information changes, and students no longer have to carry heavy bags of books to school. Teachers can also check students' progress on exercises quickly.

However, some studies suggest that students understand and remember information better when reading on paper. Spending long hours looking at screens may also cause eye strain, and students may become distracted by other apps. In addition, schools need money to buy devices and maintain networks. Many educators believe that the best approach is to use both printed and digital materials depending on the purpose of the lesson.

topic: Restaurants banning no-shows
passage:
Many restaurants suffer losses when customers make reservations but do not show up. Because restaurants prepare food and reserve tables in advance, these "no-shows" can lead to wasted food and lost income. This problem is particularly serious for small restaurants with only a few tables.

To deal with this, some restaurants have started requiring customers to provide a credit card number when they make a reservation. If customers do not arrive and do not cancel in advance, they are charged a fee. Other restaurants ask customers to pay for their meals in advance when booking. Restaurant owners say that these systems have greatly reduced the number of no-shows.

However, some customers dislike being asked for their credit card details and may choose other restaurants instead. There are also cases in which customers cannot come because of sudden illness or emergencies, and charging them may seem unfair. Some experts suggest that restaurants should send reminder messages before the reservation date and allow flexible cancellations, which can reduce no-shows without upsetting customers.

topic: Robots in elderly care
passage:
As the number of elderly people increases, many countries are facing a shortage of care workers. To help deal with this problem, some nursing homes have introduced robots. Some robots help lift patients out of bed, while others talk with residents, remind them to take their medicine, or lead simple exercises.

Supporters say that robots can reduce the physical burden on care workers, who often suffer back injuries from lifting patients. Robots that can hold conversations may also help residents feel less lonely, and some studies have found that they can improve residents' mood and encourage them to be more active.

However, robots are often expensive to buy and maintain, and many nursing homes cannot afford them. Some care workers find the machines difficult to use and worry that they take time away from caring for residents. Critics also argue that robots cannot replace human contact and that relying on them too much could reduce the quality of care. Experts say robots should be used to support, not replace, human caregivers.

topic: Banning cars near schools
passage:
In some cities, roads around schools are now closed to cars during the times when children arrive and leave. These programs, often called "school streets," aim to make the area safer and healthier for students. Parents who drive their children to school must park further away and walk the rest of the way.

Supporters say that school streets reduce the risk of traffic accidents and lower air pollution around schools, which is especially harmful to children. They also encourage more children to walk or cycle to school, which helps them get regular exercise. Some studies have found that the number of children walking to school increased after the programs began.

However, some residents who live on the closed streets complain that the restrictions make it difficult for them to leave or return home by car. Critics also say that traffic may simply move to nearby roads, causing congestion and pollution there. Experts suggest that cities should consult residents carefully and improve walking and cycling routes before introducing school streets.

topic: Shared office spaces
passage:
Shared office spaces, sometimes called coworking spaces, have become common in many cities. Instead of renting their own office, freelancers, small businesses, and even employees of large companies can rent a desk in a shared space by the day or month. These spaces usually provide internet access, meeting rooms, and kitchens.

Users say that shared offices are cheaper and more flexible than renting a traditional office. They also provide opportunities to meet people from different industries, which can lead to new business ideas and partnerships. For people who work from home, using a shared office can help them separate their work and private lives.

However, shared offices have some disadvantages. They can be noisy, and it may be difficult to have private conversations or protect confidential information. Popular spaces may also become crowded, making it hard to find a desk. In addition, the cost of using a shared office every day can add up over time. Some companies now combine working from home with occasional use of shared offices to balance cost and convenience.

topic: Corporate volunteer days
passage:
A growing number of companies now give employees paid days off to take part in volunteer activities. Employees may help at food banks, clean up parks, or teach children at local schools. Some companies organize group activities, while others allow employees to choose an organization themselves.

Companies say that these programs benefit both society and their own business. Volunteering can improve the company's reputation in the community, and employees often return to work feeling more motivated. Working with colleagues from other departments outside the office can also help build better relationships within the company.

Critics, however, argue that such programs are sometimes used mainly for public relations, with companies advertising their good deeds while making little real impact. Some charities also say that short visits by large groups of untrained volunteers can create extra work for their staff. Experts suggest that companies should work closely with charities to understand their needs, and encourage employees to use their professional skills, such as accounting or web design, rather than only offering simple manual labor.

topic: Late-night convenience store hours
passage:
In Japan, many convenience stores have traditionally stayed open 24 hours a day. However, in recent years, some store owners have started to close their shops late at night. A shortage of part-time workers has made it difficult for owners to find staff for night shifts, and some owners have had to work long hours themselves.

Stores that have shortened their hours say that the change has reduced labor costs and improved the health of owners and employees. Because there are relatively few customers late at night in some areas, the loss of sales has been smaller than expected. Closing at night also saves electricity.

On the other hand, some customers rely on convenience stores at night, including people who work late and those who need to buy food or medicine in an emergency. In some areas, convenience stores also act as safe places for people who feel threatened at night. For this reason, some companies are testing unmanned stores that use cameras and automated payment systems so that they can remain open without staff.

topic: Learning a second foreign language
passage:
In many schools, students study English as their main foreign language. However, some educators believe that students should also have the opportunity to learn a second foreign language, such as Chinese, Korean, or Spanish. In some countries, learning two foreign languages is already a standard part of secondary education.

Supporters argue that learning another language helps students understand different cultures and prepares them for an increasingly global job market. Languages of neighboring countries can be especially useful for business and tourism. Some research also suggests that learning multiple languages can improve students' thinking skills and memory.

However, critics point out that many students still struggle to reach a high level in English, and adding another language could reduce the time available for it. Schools may also find it difficult to hire qualified teachers for less common languages. Experts suggest that a second foreign language could be offered as an optional subject, allowing interested students to study it without increasing the burden on everyone.
